items.definition: A timed test of logic, numeracy or language, often given before or after the first interview.
items.example: The second stage was a numerical aptitude test with forty questions.

items.definition: A trial period at the start of a contract, often three or six months, when either side can end the arrangement.
items.example: The contract starts with a three-month probation period.

items.definition: The amount of time you must give before leaving a job, commonly one or two months.
items.example: I can give one month's notice, so I could start in April.

items.definition: A person your former employer allows a new employer to contact to check your work history.
items.example: Could you give me a reference from your last manager?

items.definition: An ability that counts in a new job even when the industry or the title is different.
items.example: Project coordination is a transferable skill, whatever the sector.

items.definition: Any person or group affected by a decision, inside or outside the organisation.
items.example: I had to keep three stakeholders updated without overloading them.

items.definition: An interview question about something you actually did in the past, usually answered with a specific example.
items.example: That was a behavioural question, so she should give a real story, not a general principle.

items.definition: A regular discussion of your pay, often once a year, separate from a performance review.
items.example: My pay review is at the end of March, so I asked to be included.

items.definition: A formal conversation with your manager about your work and how you are doing, usually held before a pay review.
items.example: I had a strong performance review, and I want to use it in my pay case.

items.definition: The range a role is paid within, with a minimum, a midpoint and a maximum.
items.example: My band goes from $1,400 to $1,900, and I am currently below the midpoint.

items.definition: The middle figure of a pay band, usually the point where an employee is expected to be fully competent.
items.example: I am about $120 below the midpoint for my band.

items.definition: A figure used to compare your pay with the market rate for the same role.
items.example: The benchmark for this role in Hanoi is around $1,750.

items.definition: Everything you receive from a job: salary, bonus, allowances and benefits, not only the monthly pay.
items.example: My total compensation is $1,650, including the transport allowance.

items.definition: A payment that depends on results, usually agreed at the start of the year.
items.example: I asked whether a higher bonus could work instead of a permanent increase.

items.definition: A single increase to pay that does not change your base salary.
items.example: They offered a one-off adjustment of $150 for this year.

items.definition: An increase given to bring pay in line with the market, framed as a fix rather than a reward.
items.example: The company called it a market correction, which is still a pay rise.

items.definition: A change of level within the same job, which usually comes with a pay band change.
items.example: They suggested a regrade to senior analyst.

items.definition: A payment made to an employee when a job ends, often calculated by years of service.
items.example: The package included three months of salary as severance.

items.definition: To respond to an offer with a different figure, as in a negotiation.
items.example: They offered $1,650, so I countered with $1,800.

items.definition: Raising your own standing by showing that another person cannot do the work.
items.example: It was competence shaming: a real error became the reason to put her down in front of the team.

items.definition: The place a person holds in a group: the respect and the authority that other people give them.
items.example: Her status in the room changed the moment she was corrected in front of the client.

items.definition: The part of a person's standing that says their word about their own work can be trusted.
items.example: A public correction took her credibility away, and it took months to get it back.

items.definition: A correction of somebody's work made in front of other people, where the correction also lowers their standing.
items.example: The public correction in the review meeting lasted a minute and stayed with her for a month.

items.definition: Saying that something may be wrong without ever saying what is right, so that the doubt stays open.
items.example: The hedging ran for weeks: doubt after doubt, and never one confirmed number.

items.definition: The people who are present and watching when you act.
items.example: With the customer in the room, the audience changed what he said.

items.definition: The act of lowering the value that other people attach to a person's work or judgement.
items.example: The devaluation was quiet: every meeting began with a small doubt about her work.

items.definition: The work a person does to keep their place and their standing in a group.
items.example: Status maintenance is why she read the report twice before she sent it.

items.definition: The slow, repeated work of taking away a person's confidence in their own judgement.
items.example: The undermining was a few small remarks spread over a month, and none of them alone was worth arguing with.

items.definition: Letting a person keep their standing, especially after a mistake or a failure.
items.example: The manager saved face by letting the report be corrected without naming who had written it.

items.definition: The public standing a person carries at work: the regard of colleagues, clients and the team.
items.example: His professional face was in pieces for a month after the review.

items.definition: Turning a question back on the person who asked it, so that the original question is never answered.
items.example: The deflection worked once, and I still had not answered what was wrong with the drawing.

items.definition: The arrangement in which one person is placed below another and kept there.
items.example: The subordination was taught in the meeting: whoever spoke second was corrected first.

items.definition: The use of pressure, ambiguity or emotion to move a person into a decision that does not serve them, without giving a real choice.
items.example: It was manipulation: he offered her two options and made the wrong one impossible.

items.definition: An error in the shape of an argument, a move that breaks the reasoning instead of answering the claim.
items.example: Calling the move a fallacy describes it; it does not insult the person.

items.definition: The presenting of two options as if no other option existed.
items.example: Either we cut the budget by a third, or the service stops — that is a false dilemma.

items.definition: A question that carries its own answer inside its wording.
items.example: When will you stop making excuses? is a loaded question.

items.definition: The moving of the criterion after the other side has met it.
items.example: Three sources were required, then written external sources were required: that was goalpost shifting.

items.definition: The replacing of a reason with a feeling, and the treatment of the feeling as the answer.
items.example: After everything I have done for this team was an appeal to emotion, not a reason.

items.definition: The replacing of a reason with the title or the status of the person who offers it.
items.example: The chief engineer says it is safe was an appeal to authority, because no evidence was shown.

items.definition: An argument that nobody made, set up so that it can be knocked down easily.
items.example: So you want to drop the whole project was a straw man; the speaker had only said the schedule was short.
